newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Pre-election violence spreads in Albanian south.
newsitem.headline: Pre-election violence spreads in Albanian south.

text.p: Albania's chaotic south slid deeper into anarchy on Thursday as the country's finance minister narrowly escaped from a gunbattle in the southern port of Vlore three days ahead of a general election.

Arben Malaj was forced to take shelter in a nearby seaside hotel after rival local warlords exchanged volleys of gunfire during an election rally held in the town's dilapidated sports palace, which was later set on fire.

A statement by the Italian-led international protection force released in the capital Tirana said two platoons and two armoured personnel carriers were dispatched to evacuate civilians from the smouldering building.
Witnesses said the Italians did not open fire. Calm appeared to return to the area, though sporadic shooting could still be heard in other parts of the town of 90,000 people.

Local police earlier said one person had died and two were injured during the day's violence, a regular feature in many parts of the impoverished nation after a string of dubious pyramid funds folded earlier this year.
Sunday's snap elections, pitting President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party against the Socialists, are widely regarded as the last chance to restore peace in the troubled Balkan state.
With thousands of weapons looted from army depots now in the hands of criminal gangs and teenagers, more than 1,500 people have been killed this year.

In the southern town of Sarande, a candidate for the Union of Human Rights party that represents the region's large ethnic Greek minority told Reuters her father had been seized near Gjirokaster, a town about 60 km (40 miles) to the northeast.

Konstandina Bezhani said she had received a call from men claiming to hold her father who told her to withdraw from the parliamentary race if she wanted to see him again. Her father was one of five ethnic Greeks arrested for a time in 1994 on suspicion of illegal weapons possession and spying for Greece.
Like most of southern Albania, Saranda and Vlore are run by "Salvation Committees" violently opposed to Berisha and hoping the election will force him from office.
But the election has been threatened by the outbreak of daily street battles between gangs, with residents scurrying inside at the sound of a warning siren.
Vlore was the starting point in January of largely spontaneous protests by unsuspecting investors who lost their life savings in the collapse of the fraudulent schemes.
Angry protesters blamed the calamity on Berisha, who is campaigning to defend a huge majority his Democratic Party won in last year's parliamentary ballot.
Opposition Socialist rallies still chant "Vlore, Vlore!" as a symbol of resistance to the president.
Berisha's Democrats say they dare not set foot in the port. His opponents warn of unstoppable violence if Berisha remains in place after the vote.
"The people will vote and they will remove Berisha," said Albert Shyti, a former rebel leader in Vlore who is now running for parliament for the opposition Social Democrats.
"If they don't remove him with their votes, they will take up their guns and remove him with their guns."

From the furious, but principled protests of January, Vlore has descended into a daily cauldron of tactical street warfare, where masked fighters use trees, posts and gutted cars to stake out territorial advantage.

Salvation Committee members this week met Italian troops and observers of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), overseeing the elections, to try to patch together arrangements for safe voting.
But many residents have little hope that will happen.
"Now we have fighting every day," said one elderly man. "How can we possibly vote safely?"
